posts.reason: Builds on Blum's finite-automaton remark and Lamport's line on thinking without writing to give five concrete writing rules, and argues that writing your own prose is now an advantage over LLM text.
A philosopher-backed argument, drawing on Longino, Brandom and Thurston, that verified results only become knowledge through accountability, criticism and human understanding.

Original national-accounts calculations and a reproducible model behind the claim that output per hour rose 2.5 times since 1973 while ordinary pay buys 19 percent more, ending in a case for a common ownership dividend.
A concrete account of turning an app's internals into a 1.0 library: a stable C ABI, semantic versioning, ABI checks enforced in CI, packaging for distributions, and a 10,000-terminal load test.

Argues by reductio that engineers keep their leverage over coding agents through problem framing, a sense of what will age badly and Polanyi-style tacit knowledge, and the 310-comment thread brings first-hand reports from senior engineers.

Paul Ford makes the case that browser APIs like WebAssembly, WebGL and Web Crypto already make the web a full app platform, and practitioners in the thread compare their own browser builds, including Three.js against vanilla WebGL.
A 20,000-word history-and-travel essay on how a tiny republic survived thirteen invasion or annexation attempts, a fascist period, a semi-communist government and a banking collapse.

Lists four causes and four symptoms of fragility in AI-heavy codebases from experience rather than data, and the 625-comment thread sets similar reports against people whose AI-written code works fine.

A long-time Claude Code user explains a move to the open-source Pi harness with specifics: lost editor selections, prompt changes across 244 releases and a Bash tool description of nearly 3,000 tokens.
Jane Street's short note that some interview rounds now test software design, verifying code and working with LLMs; the thread is a debate over what coding screens still measure.

Reads the Peter Principle through a study of careers under dictatorship, arguing that leaders promoted past their competence may turn to dirty work to protect their position, with a thread on separate technical and management tracks.

Maciej Cegłowski works through space radiation, the Tanpopo ISS experiment, permafrost and a disputed 250-million-year-old bacterium to argue that contamination control is the real bottleneck for Mars samples.
